title_original: $6.5M Jan Brueghel Sells at Frieze in London as Collectors Compete for Coveted Works
excerpt_original: Some galleries enjoyed triumphant returns, the big guys reported big sales, and others were still seeking heat.

blocks.text: “It’s hard to buy right now,” one prominent millennial London collector sighed, rolling back his head in frustration. By which he meant: It’s hard to get access to the most desirable work. Yet, for many dealers at the VIP opening of Frieze London today , it remained hard to sell, too. More than ever, excitement is concentrated in “heat pockets,” advisor Nico Epstein said.

One of this year’s heat pockets is the booth of London dealer Pilar Corrias , who is enjoying a triumphant return following a two-year hiatus to focus on Art Basel Paris . Her three-person booth featured sprawling, otherworldly landscapes by local painters Sholto Blissett and Georg Wilson , as well as Rachel Rose , from New York. Everything sold.

Even access to the PDF for British abstract painter Francesca Mollett ’s solo presentation with Modern Art (London, Paris) was tightly controlled, one advisor told me. No need to advertise too widely when there are already several contenders for every one of the works, which are priced between £15,000 and £100,000 ($20,000–$130,000).

The social whirl of Frieze London was, as always, frenetic. One of my interviews was interrupted by occasional performance artist Tilda Swinton . Other celeb sightings included actors Andrew Garfield , Pedro Pascal , and Helena Bonham Carter . Big-name collectors were here, too, like Don and Mera Rubell , Pamela Joyner , Chris Walker , and Kent Kelley .

Amid the recent market contraction, many fairs have shrunk or shifted their focus to home regions. Everyone agrees that, in a competitive global landscape, London’s art industry needs to stay savvy and open to new opportunities. Rising markets in the Global South are still in need of major international footholds, and the city may be well placed to serve that role, thanks to its strong historical ties with South Asia and the Gulf. Some market makers are also eyeing Latin America.
“Most Americans now like to visit Paris,” for Art Basel, advisor Nayrouz Tatanaki said . “London is more for the rest of the world.”

Next month, Frieze will make its debut in Abu Dhabi. “Everyone says we are crazy,” its CEO, Simon Fox , joked during a dinner hosted by Ruinart on Tuesday evening. The fair’s imperial ambitions may pay dividends. Ahead of today’s opening, VIP bookings were up 24 percent from the MENA region (Middle East and North Africa), 22 percent from South Asia, and 22 percent from Southeast Asia, compared to last year, according to the fair.

Tatanaki said that many of her Arab and South Asian buyers have second homes in London, and even those who fled the U.K. following Labour’s changes to its tax regime in April 2025 are returning in force for Frieze.

Advisor Morgan Long told me that the choice between London and Paris often simply comes down to which exhibitions a collector would rather see. There is ambitious, globally relevant programming in the British capital right now, including the Serpentine ‘s major solo exhibition with Indian filmmaker Amar Kanwar , Tate Modern ‘s Turbine Hall commission with Lebanese artist-composer Tarek Atoui , Anish Kapoor at the Hayward Gallery , and Salman Toor at the Courtauld .

Mumbai’s Project 88 has been doing Frieze since 2009, when it was the only Indian gallery, and it has never been easier for it to align its booth with institutional happenings around town. Today, it sold two editions of a 2015 photo series by Munem Wasif that is currently on display at Tate Modern for between £15,000 and £20,000, as well as three sculptures in the same range by Amol K. Patil , who recently exhibited at the Hayward .
Sold in the region of £5 million by Hauser & Wirth: Jan Brueghel the Elder, Still Life of Flowers in a Stoneware Vase , ca. 1607–08. Photo: Eva Herzog

Vadehra Art Gallery , of New Delhi, sold two Sunil Gupta photographs priced between $8,000 and $10,000 to an institution. The artist is currently being exhibited at Kettle’s Yard in Cambridge. More works by Atul Dodiya , Biraaj Dodiya , Sudhir Patwardhan , and Zaam Arif sold to collectors from L.A., Copenhagen, and London for $30,000–$80,000.

VIP bookings from Brazil were up 36 percent, perhaps because of the rise in the number of exhibitors from the country. Just one, Vermelho from São Paulo, exhibited in the main section in 2022, compared to four this time. They include Fortes D’Aloia & Gabriel , a once-dedicated Frieze exhibitor that dropped out during the pandemic, then swapped London for Paris. It was lured back by last year’s curated section, which spotlighted Brazilian art. This year, its presentation of emerging artist Márcia Falcão is the first thing you’ll see on entering the fair. All five paintings sold: two for $30,000 each and three more for $60,000 apiece. São Paulo’s Simões de Assis , meanwhile, sold works by Thalita Hamaoui priced between $30,000 and $50,000.
Things were quieter at Masters, where the pace usually runs a little slower, though some dealers toward the back of the tent were getting antsy for more footfall by 2 p.m.

Late in the day, Hauser & Wirth confirmed the sale of a Jan Brueghel the Elder still life “in the region of” £5 million ($6.5 million). The painting, once owned by Baron Alphonse von Rothschild , previously sold in 2016 at Sotheby’s in London for £3.8 million ($4.96 million at the time).

blocks.text: Installation view of Loft Gallery’s presentation of paintings by Mohamed Melehi at Frieze Masters, 2026. Courtesy of Loft Art Gallery.

Several galleries from MENA were present, courting Western institutions ahead of Frieze Abu Dhabi. Casablanca’s Loft Art Gallery made its Frieze debut in the curated Spotlight sector, which is dedicated to solo presentations of 20th-century artists. It brought works by Mohamed Melehi , a defining figure of Moroccan modernism and the Casablanca School whose vibrant wave-patterned paintings are in important international collections.

“Melehi has opened the way for other Moroccan artists,” Loft’s cofounder, Yasmin Berrada , said, noting that the market for Moroccan art has internationalized significantly since she started working with the artist 11 years ago. (He died in 2020 at the age of 83.) “It used to be that only Moroccan collectors bought Moroccan art, but that’s not the case anymore.” Works at the booth ranged from €130,000 to €400,000 ($145,500 to $447,700); two were on hold by lunchtime.

A few stalls away, Dubai’s Lawrie Shabibi was showing intricate works on paper by the Palestinian artist Maliheh Afnan , whose work has not been widely shown since her death in London in 2016 at the age of 80. Moonshine (1988), the priciest work on the stand at £70,000 ($92,700), had yet to sell. It is a close cousin of Nocturnal City (1987), a recent acquisition by Tate Modern.

Jeddah, Saudi Arabia’s ATHR gallery was participating in Masters for the first time, in the main galleries section, with a presentation of two pioneers of Saudi modernism, Mounirah Mosly , who died in 2019 at 64, and 72-year-old Abdulrahman AlSoliman . The pairing marks a notable expansion of the gallery’s program, which until now has focused mainly on younger contemporary artists. Mosly’s works are priced “above £100,000,” he said, but AlSoliman’s are “more accessible,” in the five-figure range. The works were still awaiting buyers.

Blue-chip heavyweights had no trouble shifting the usual fare, of course. Hauser & Wirth also sold an $800,000 Avery Singer , and White Cube sold five paintings by Ilana Savdie for between $110,000 and $175,000. Perrotin sold several Izumi Kato paintings and sculptures for up to $250,000 each; David Zwirner moved a $1.5 million Michaël Borremans and a $900,000 Dana Schutz . The biggest hit at Karma was a $350,000 Gertrude Abercrombie , and Thaddaeus Ropac sold an Anthony Gormley for £500,000 ($657,000) and a Martha Jungwirth for €590,000 ($655,000).
Frieze runs in Regent’s Park through Sunday. Then it’s on to Paris.
Margaret Carrigan contributed reporting.
